title: The Man Who Never Boarded a Ship: Praeneste, Rome, and Seventeen Books of Animals
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Praeneste, Under the Terraces of Fortune

stops.name: Praeneste, birth below the oracle
stops.date_confidence: Year is a modern deduction, not an ancient date. The Oxford Classical Dictionary brackets 161/177; Wikipedia gives c. 175. The month and day are unknown and defaulted to 01-01. Praeneste itself is attested: the Suda, entry alpha-iota 178, opens 'Of Praeneste in Italy.'
stops.campa: A son is born at Praeneste in Latium, twenty-three miles east of Rome, on the mountain slope where the terraces of Fortuna Primigenia climb in ramps and colonnades above the plain. The town speaks Latin, and every surviving word he wrote is Greek. The Suda, compiling seven centuries later, gives the town and almost nothing else: 'Of Praeneste in Italy. High-priest and sophist; surnamed Claudius.' No inscription names his father, and no document gives a trade or a day.
stops.quote: Of Praeneste in Italy. High-priest and sophist; surnamed Claudius. He was nicknamed 'honey-tongued' or 'honey-voiced'. He was a sophist in Rome itself in the period after Hadrian.
stops.quote_source: Suda, entry alpha-iota 178 (s.v. Ailianos), Suda On Line translation
suggested_refs: Suda On Line, entry alpha-iota 178, the four sentences that carry the whole of his origin
Modern Palestrina, Lazio, the site of ancient Praeneste
sources: Suda On Line, entry alpha-iota 178, https://cs.uky.edu/~raphael/sol/sol-entries/alphaiota/178
Wikipedia, 'Aelian (writer)'
M. B. Trapp, Oxford Classical Dictionary, 'Aelian' (cited at second hand; academic.oup.com returned 403)

stops.name: Praeneste, the sanctuary of Fortuna Primigenia
stops.date_confidence: Undated and unattested for Aelian personally. No ancient source places him in the sanctuary. The terraces, the oracular lots and the Nile mosaic are the town's own attested furniture; the date orders the segment only.
stops.campa: The sanctuary above the town is the largest in Italy: terrace upon terrace of ramps and porticoes carrying the oracle of Fortuna Primigenia, First-Born Fortune, whose lots are drawn from a chest of oak and read out to whoever has climbed the hill for them. Any boy of the town can walk up into it. In the eastern nymphaeum, Alexandrian workmen have laid a mosaic floor that maps the Nile from the Ethiopian highlands down to the delta, with hippopotamus and crocodile and ibis set among the temples and the reed boats.
suggested_refs: The Nile mosaic of the eastern nymphaeum, Palestrina, attributed to Alexandrian workmen of the late second century BC
The terraced Sanctuary of Fortuna Primigenia, Palestrina
sources: Wikipedia, 'Palestrina, Lazio', on the Nile mosaic and the nymphaeum
Cicero, De divinatione 2.85-87, on the sortes of Praeneste and the oaken chest

stops.name: Praeneste, the priesthood the Suda names
stops.date_confidence: Attested as a title, unattested as to cult, city, or date. The Suda says archiereus, high priest, and nothing further. The placement at Praeneste is a modern conjecture; C. W. Marshall, reviewing Steven D. Smith, warns that this one biographical detail has been over-invested with meaning.
stops.campa: The Suda gives him one office and no cult: archiereus, high priest. It does not say of what god, or in what city, or under which emperor. Praeneste has the great oracle and Rome has a hundred priesthoods, and the single word covers both. Readers who want the sanctuary of Fortune to explain his lifelong appetite for portents and monstrous births must supply the connection themselves, because the four sentences the Suda spends on him supply nothing. Priest of what god, and in which city?
suggested_refs: Steven D. Smith, Man and Animal in Severan Rome (Cambridge, 2014), on the priesthood as a key to the work
Bryn Mawr Classical Review 2015.09.15 (C. W. Marshall), on the same detail as over-invested
sources: Suda On Line, entry alpha-iota 178
Bryn Mawr Classical Review 2015.09.15, https://bmcr.brynmawr.edu/2015/2015.09.15/

segments.name: The Attic Tongue in the Latin City

stops.name: Rome, the pupil of Pausanias
stops.date_confidence: The relation is attested, the date is not. Philostratus, Lives of the Sophists 2.31: 'He was a pupil of Pausanias.' No source gives a year, a place of instruction, or a length of study; the date orders the segment.
stops.campa: He comes to Rome for the training a Greek education demands, and Philostratus names one teacher only: Pausanias of Caesarea, a sophist of the Atticizing school, whose business is the recovery of a Greek four hundred years dead. The lesson takes. Aelian will spend his working life inside a Latin city, hearing Latin in the courts and the markets, and composing in the vocabulary and the syntax of classical Athens. Philostratus names no school for the instruction, no year, no length of study and no fellow pupil.
suggested_refs: Philostratus, Lives of the Sophists 2.31, the Life of Aelian entire, two pages long
sources: Philostratus, Lives of the Sophists 2.31, trans. Wilmer Cave Wright, Loeb Classical Library 134 (1922), p. 307, scanned at archive.org, identifier philostratuseuna00phil

stops.name: Rome, Attic as the Athenians of the interior
stops.date_confidence: The judgment is attested; the date is an ordering device. Philostratus wrote his Lives in the 230s, looking back over Aelian's whole career, and does not date the assessment.
stops.campa: Philostratus opens his notice with the thing his readers would find strange first: the man is a Roman. The Greek is not a second language worn thin over a first. It is exact and free of the provinces, the Attic of the inland demes rather than of the port. Sophists arrive in Rome from Smyrna and Ephesus and Athens with the language in their mouths from birth; this one has it out of books and out of Pausanias, and on the page the difference does not show. The Suda records the nickname it earned him: honey-tongued.
stops.quote: Aelian was a Roman, but he wrote Attic as correctly as the Athenians in the interior of Attica.
stops.quote_source: Philostratus, Lives of the Sophists 2.31, trans. Wilmer Cave Wright, Loeb Classical Library 134 (1922)
suggested_refs: The Atticizing programme of the Second Sophistic, against which Aelian's Greek was measured
sources: Philostratus, Lives of the Sophists 2.31 (Wright, Loeb 134, 1922), archive.org identifier philostratuseuna00phil
Suda On Line, entry alpha-iota 178, for the nickname 'honey-tongued'

stops.name: Rome, the title of sophist taken without trust
stops.date_confidence: Attested without a date. Philostratus, VS 2.31: he received the title from those who award that honour, but did not trust the honour or let it flatter him. The year is an ordering device inside the Severan decades the Suda assigns him.
stops.campa: The title of sophist is granted in the Severan capital by men with the standing to grant it, and it is granted to him. Philostratus records what he did with it: nothing. He does not trust the honour, and he does not build the career it opens. Around him the profession is public and loud, with fortunes and civic honours riding on a morning's improvisation: the speaker on his feet in front of a crowd, taking a theme shouted up from the floor and answering it without preparation.
suggested_refs: The Athenaeum of Hadrian near the modern Piazza Madonna di Loreto, the best-attested venue for sophistic declamation in Severan Rome, though Philostratus names no building for Aelian
sources: Philostratus, Lives of the Sophists 2.31 (Wright, Loeb 134, 1922)
Suda On Line, entry alpha-iota 178, placing his sophistic practice at Rome after Hadrian

stops.name: Rome, Herodes Atticus admired across a generation
stops.date_confidence: The admiration is attested, the date is not. Philostratus, VS 2.31: 'he admired Herodes as the most various of orators', Greek poikilotaton rhetoron. Herodes died in 177; the chronologies make instruction implausible and Philostratus claims none. No source places Aelian in Athens, and this stop is set at his own Rome pin for that reason.
stops.campa: Of all the orators he could have named he names Herodes Atticus, and calls him poikilotatos, the most various. Variety is the quality he will build his own book on, a work that refuses to sort its animals by kind or country, that sets the elephant next to the ant because the eye tires of order. Herodes died at Marathon in 177, before Aelian had a career of his own. There was no meeting, and no voice was ever heard. Philostratus reports the admiration and claims nothing further.
suggested_refs: Philostratus, Lives of the Sophists, the Life of Herodes Atticus (VS 2.1)
The Odeon of Herodes Atticus, Athens, built by the orator Aelian admired and never visited
sources: Philostratus, Lives of the Sophists 2.31 (Wright, Loeb 134, 1922), p. 307

stops.name: Rome, the turn from the platform to the desk
stops.date_confidence: Attested as a fact, undated as an event. Philostratus, VS 2.31: judging his own abilities unsuited to declamation, he applied himself to writing history and won admiration in it. The year is an ordering device.
stops.campa: He judges his own abilities and finds them wrong for declamation. Philostratus puts it without cruelty and without disguise: the gifts were not suited to it, so he applied himself to writing history and won admiration in that instead. It is a decision made against the whole grain of the Second Sophistic, which rewards the voice and the crowd. He takes the desk. Seventeen books on animals and fourteen books of anecdotes come out of it, and they are what survives of him.
suggested_refs: Aelian, Varia Historia, the fourteen books of anecdotes, surviving in abridged form
sources: Philostratus, Lives of the Sophists 2.31 (Wright, Loeb 134, 1922)
N. G. Wilson, introduction to Aelian, Historical Miscellany, Loeb Classical Library 486 (1997), on the abridgement and the posthumous release

stops.name: Rome, the man who never boarded a ship
stops.date_confidence: Attested as a saying repeated over a career, not as a dated event. Philostratus, VS 2.31, reports that Aelian used to say it and that Rome esteemed him the more for it. The date orders the segment.
stops.campa: He tells people, and lets it be repeated, that he has never gone outside the confines of Italy, never set foot on a ship, never known the sea. Philostratus reports that Rome esteemed him the more for it, taking the refusal as a compliment to their own way of living. The claim sits underneath everything he wrote. Seventeen books cross India, Persia, Taprobane, Ethiopia and the upper Nile, and they are composed, on their author's own account, by a man whose feet never left the peninsula.
suggested_refs: Aelian, On the Characteristics of Animals 11.40, the one passage in which he claims to have seen something in Egypt
sources: Philostratus, Lives of the Sophists 2.31 (Wright, Loeb 134, 1922)

segments.name: Marvels Brought by Report: the East of the Book

stops.name: The Indus frontier, the Dog-heads of India
stops.date_confidence: The text is attested; the pin is editorial. Aelian, On Animals 4.46, says only 'in the same part of India as the beetles' and names no city or river. Taxila on the Indus frontier stands for the Indian country of the Greek sources. The date is the conventional composition window, not an event.
stops.campa: In the Indian country, in the same chapters as the beetles, he sets the Dog-heads. They are shaped like men, walk upright, wear the skins of animals and injure nobody. They cannot speak, but they howl, and they understand what is said to them in Indian. He files them among the beasts and gives his reason: the sound is inarticulate, and it is not the sound of a man. Ctesias put them in a book seven centuries earlier and Aelian works from that line of copying. They keep goats and sheep and drink the milk, and their game is not cooked on a fire but shredded and laid out in the sun.
stops.quote: For the rest they are of human shape and go about clothed in the skins of beasts; and they are upright and injure no man; and though they have no speech they howl; yet they understand the Indian language.
stops.quote_source: Aelian, On the Characteristics of Animals 4.46, trans. A. F. Scholfield, via Attalus.org
suggested_refs: Ctesias of Cnidus, Indica, surviving through Photius, Bibliotheca cod. 72, the earliest source for the Indian dog-headed people
Pliny, Natural History 7.2.22-23, transmitting Megasthenes on the same creatures
sources: Aelian, On the Characteristics of Animals 4.46, https://www.attalus.org/translate/animals4.html
ToposText, Aelian, On Animals, work 560

stops.name: Susa, Ctesias vouched for and doubted in one breath
stops.date_confidence: Aelian's text is attested; the pin belongs to Ctesias, physician at the Persian court, which is where the report Aelian is quoting was gathered. Aelian says only 'in Persia'. Date is the composition window.
stops.campa: The Martichoras is red as cinnabar, the size of the largest lion, shaggy as a dog, and its face is a man's. Ctesias of Cnidus, physician at the Persian court, says he saw one himself, brought from India as a present for the King. Aelian copies the claim out and attaches a condition to it in the same sentence: if Ctesias is to be regarded as a sufficient authority on such matters. He does not strike the beast from the book. He leaves it standing with the doubt fastened to it, in the same sentence, where a reader cannot miss it. Whether he believed the thing himself, the text does not say.
stops.quote: Ctesias declares that he has actually seen this animal in Persia (it had been brought from India as a present to the Persian King) - if Ctesias is to be regarded as a sufficient authority on such matters.
stops.quote_source: Aelian, On the Characteristics of Animals 4.21, trans. A. F. Scholfield, via Attalus.org
suggested_refs: Ctesias of Cnidus at the court of Artaxerxes II, the source Aelian names and qualifies
sources: Aelian, On the Characteristics of Animals 4.21, https://www.attalus.org/translate/animals4.html
ctesias.journey.json, stop 'Susa, the men who bark', for the canonical Susa pin

stops.name: Pataliputra, the one-horned foals of the Prasian king
stops.date_confidence: Text attested at On Animals 16.20-21; the pin is editorial, since Aelian names the King of the Prasii and no city. Pataliputra is the Prasian capital of the Greek sources. Colunda, the wooded country of the satyrs, cannot be pinned at all and is folded into this stop rather than given an invented coordinate.
stops.campa: At the capital of the Prasii, on the Ganges, the king's shows put young Cartazoni against one another: one-horned, horse-maned, reddish, the horn black and spiralled and grown that way rather than worked. Nobody, Aelian notes, remembers a full-grown one being taken. From the wooded country called Colunda beyond the frontier mountains come the shaggy horse-tailed creatures he calls Satyrs, who fight by rolling rocks down on whoever climbs after them; the ones that reach the king are the sick and the pregnant. Megasthenes went to this court as an ambassador, and Aelian works from what men like him carried home.
stops.quote: the foals when quite young are taken to the King of the Prasii and exhibit their strength one against another in the public shows, but nobody remembers a full-grown animal having been captured.
stops.quote_source: Aelian, On the Characteristics of Animals 16.20, trans. A. F. Scholfield, via Attalus.org
suggested_refs: Megasthenes, Indica, written from the Mauryan court at Pataliputra, the ambassadorial source behind the Greek picture of the Prasii
sources: Aelian, On the Characteristics of Animals 16.20-21, https://www.attalus.org/translate/animals16.html
megasthenes.journey.json, for the corpus treatment of the Indica

stops.name: Taprobane, the sea-beings with women's faces
stops.date_confidence: Text attested at On Animals 16.17-19. The pin is Mantai on the Mannar coast of Sri Lanka, the classical landfall of Taprobane; Aelian names no harbour. Date is the composition window.
stops.campa: Off Taprobane, in water he places at the far edge of the map, he reports beings with the bodies of satyrs and the faces of women, spines standing where hair should be, tails immense and coiling, claws or fins instead of feet. They are amphibious, living in the water and feeding on the land. At night they come up to graze the fields and the date palms, and at first light the ocean takes them back. No witness is named, no boat, no date. The chapter runs straight on to the next marvel.
suggested_refs: Taprobane in the Greek geographers, the outermost island of the inhabited world
sources: Aelian, On the Characteristics of Animals 16.17-19, https://www.attalus.org/translate/animals16.html

stops.name: Rome, the Hydra set aside and the Amphisbaena kept
stops.date_confidence: Text attested at On Animals 9.23. Placed at Aelian's own Rome pin because it is a statement of method rather than a location in the book. Date is the composition window.
stops.campa: He draws a line, and it is not the line a modern reader expects. The Hydra of Lerna and the three-headed Chimaera belong to poets and to the compilers of ancient legends, and he consigns them to the region of myths. The Amphisbaena he keeps, because it is a snake with a head at each end and a snake is a thing that can be reported. The distinction is not between the credible and the incredible. Poets invented the Hydra. Somebody claims to have met an Amphisbaena.
stops.quote: Now these seem to have been relegated to the region of myths. The Amphisbaena however is a snake with two heads, one at the top and one in the direction of the tail.
stops.quote_source: Aelian, On the Characteristics of Animals 9.23, trans. A. F. Scholfield, via Attalus.org
suggested_refs: Hecataeus of Miletus and Homer, the authorities Aelian names in order to set them aside
sources: Aelian, On the Characteristics of Animals 9.23, https://www.attalus.org/translate/animals9.html

segments.name: Egypt, and the Journey He Denied

stops.name: The Great Oasis, seven days of utter desert
stops.date_confidence: The text is attested; the identification is not. On Animals 10.25 names no oasis, only 'the Egyptian oasis' and the road that leads to Ethiopia. Kharga, the Great Oasis, is the one that sits on the southbound desert route toward Nubia; an earlier draft of this file placed the stop at Siwa, from which no road leads to Ethiopia, and the correction is recorded here.
stops.campa: Past the Egyptian oasis the road gives out into seven days of nothing. He names no town and no well, only the crossing and how long it takes, and then what is found on the far side of it. He has it from a man who walked it, or from a book by a man who did, and he gives neither. The route runs south from the Great Oasis toward Nubia and the country the Greeks call Ethiopia. It is the caravan road that carries ivory and animals and slaves north to the Nile.
stops.quote: After traversing the Egyptian oasis one is confronted for seven whole days with utter desert.
stops.quote_source: Aelian, On the Characteristics of Animals 10.25, trans. A. F. Scholfield, via Attalus.org
suggested_refs: The Great Oasis (Kharga and Dakhla) and the desert road south toward Nubia
sources: Aelian, On the Characteristics of Animals 10.25, https://www.attalus.org/translate/animals10.html

stops.name: Meroe, the human Dog-faces on the Ethiopian road
stops.date_confidence: Text attested at On Animals 10.25; the pin is editorial. Aelian writes only 'along the road that leads to Ethiopia' and names no place. Meroe, capital of Kush, stands for the classical Ethiopia the passage gestures toward.
stops.campa: Beyond the desert, on the road toward Ethiopia, he places the human Dog-faces. They are black-skinned, dog-headed and dog-toothed, hair over the whole body, a beard hanging under the chin that he compares to a dragon's, and their hands end in nails sharp enough to cut with. They have no speech, only a shrill squeal. They hunt gazelle and antelope and outrun anything sent after them, and they know which country cannot be entered, which is why none is ever taken. He never says these are the Indian Dog-heads of the fourth book.
stops.quote: They are however not endowed with speech, but utter a shrill squeal. Beneath their chin hangs down a beard; we may compare it with the beards of dragons, and strong and very sharp nails give an edge to their hands.
stops.quote_source: Aelian, On the Characteristics of Animals 10.25, trans. A. F. Scholfield, via Attalus.org
suggested_refs: Aelian, On Animals 4.46, the Indian Dog-heads, a separate account of separate creatures
sources: Aelian, On the Characteristics of Animals 10.25, https://www.attalus.org/translate/animals10.html

stops.name: Alexandria, the ox with five feet
stops.date_confidence: The text is attested and quoted verbatim; the visit it claims is disputed by the other surviving testimony and is left unresolved here. Aelian names no year and no temple: the offering is 'to this god', and the god is unnamed in 11.39-40. The Serapeum identification often attached to the passage is editorial, and the pin is the corpus's canonical Alexandria coordinate rather than any precinct.
stops.campa: He breaks the register he has kept for eleven books and speaks in his own person. He has seen it: a sacred ox with five feet, an offering in the great city of Alexandria, standing in the far-famed grove of the god where the persea trees are planted close and the shade is the coolest there is. He has also seen a calf with a fully formed extra foot growing from its shoulder. He closes by saying he has reported what he himself saw and heard. Philostratus, writing about him in the same decade, says the man never boarded a ship.
stops.quote: And I myself have seen a sacred ox with five feet which was an offering to this god in the great city of Alexandria, in the far-famed grove of the god, where the persea-trees close-planted afforded the loveliest shade and coolness... True, these phenomena appear far from conformity to nature, but I have reported what I myself have seen and heard.
stops.quote_source: Aelian, On the Characteristics of Animals 11.40, trans. A. F. Scholfield, via Attalus.org
suggested_refs: Philostratus, Lives of the Sophists 2.31, the statement that Aelian never left Italy or boarded a ship
strabo.journey.json, for the canonical Alexandria pin inherited here
sources: Aelian, On the Characteristics of Animals 11.40, https://www.attalus.org/translate/animals11.html
Philostratus, Lives of the Sophists 2.31 (Wright, Loeb 134, 1922)

stops.name: Sais, the lamb of Bocchoris
stops.date_confidence: Text attested at On Animals 12.3; the event it reports is legendary, set in the reign of Bocchoris (eighth century BC). The pin is the traditional royal seat associated with Bocchoris, since Aelian's text names no city. The date is the composition window, not the reign.
stops.campa: Under the pharaoh the Greeks call Bocchoris, he reports, a lamb was born with eight feet and two tails, and then again with two heads and four horns, and the creature was made to speak. He hands the story on as it reaches him and lets his own opinion show through the telling: he finds it fabulous, and says so plainly. The collector's rule is to keep the marvel and mark the doubt, and here the mark is heavier than usual. The lamb stays in the book, in the chapter with the other prodigies of the Nile kings.
suggested_refs: Bocchoris of the Twenty-fourth Dynasty and the Egyptian prodigy tradition attached to his reign
sources: Aelian, On the Characteristics of Animals 12.3, https://www.attalus.org/translate/animals12.html

stops.name: Memphis, the birds that mean a harvest
stops.date_confidence: Text attested at On Animals 11.39-40. The pin is editorial: Aelian gives no city for these omens, only Egypt and the reign of Atothis son of Menis, a legendary early dynasty. Memphis stands for Egypt broadly.
stops.campa: He gathers the Nile prodigies together as signs of abundance to come. In the reign of Atothis son of Menis a crane was born with two heads; later a bird with four; a hawk was seen with three legs, and the Egyptians read it as something sent. He is not describing monsters for their own sake in this chapter. He is recording a system in which a body that comes out wrong is a message, and the message is usually about the harvest. The three-legged hawk stands in the list with the rest, undated and unexplained.
suggested_refs: Egyptian prodigy-lists and their Greek transmission, the material behind On Animals 11.39-40
sources: Aelian, On the Characteristics of Animals 11.39-40, https://www.attalus.org/translate/animals11.html

stops.name: The Diomedean Islands, the birds that know a Greek
stops.date_confidence: Text attested at On Animals 1.1, the opening chapter of the work. The islands are the Tremiti in the Adriatic. Date is the composition window, not an event.
stops.campa: He opens the seventeen books with birds, and he opens them in Italian water, off the coast of the country he says he never left. On the Adriatic islands named for Diomedes live the transformed companions of the hero, and they can tell a Greek from a barbarian. To the barbarians they do no harm, but they will not go near them. They have kept their Greek nature and their love of Greece straight through the change of shape. To a Greek stepping ashore they come in close, extend their wings as though the wings were hands held open, and let themselves be handled.
suggested_refs: The Isole Tremiti, the Diomedean islands of the ancient geographers
sources: Aelian, On the Characteristics of Animals 1.1, https://www.attalus.org/translate/animals1.html

stops.name: Poroselene, the dolphin that swims second
stops.date_confidence: Text attested at On Animals 2.6, where the story is credited to a Byzantine named Leonidas sailing past Aeolis. The pin is Cunda (Alibey) Island, the accepted site of Pordoselene/Poroselene; an earlier draft placed it 37 km south in open water off Dikili, and the correction is recorded here.
stops.campa: At Poroselene, in the Aeolian islands off the coast opposite Lesbos, an old couple and their son raise a dolphin alongside the boy. It answers to a name. The boy stands out on a jutting rock above the water and calls it, and the animal comes in; they swim races, and the dolphin, which could take any of them, sometimes declines the winner's place and comes second instead, as though glad to be beaten. Aelian has it at second hand from a Byzantine called Leonidas, who says he sailed past and saw the thing with his own eyes.
stops.quote: he would at times even decline the winner's place and actually swim second, as though presumably he was glad to be defeated.
stops.quote_source: Aelian, On the Characteristics of Animals 2.6, trans. A. F. Scholfield, via Attalus.org
suggested_refs: Cunda (Alibey) Island off Ayvalik, the ancient Pordoselene
sources: Aelian, On the Characteristics of Animals 2.6, https://www.attalus.org/translate/animals2.html
Wikipedia, 'Cunda Island', for the coordinate and the ancient identification

stops.name: The Isthmus, the sea-crane of Corinth
stops.date_confidence: Text attested at On Animals 15.9. The pin is Isthmia at the Corinthian isthmus; an earlier draft placed it 18 km east out in the Saronic Gulf, and the correction is recorded here.
stops.campa: In the water off Corinth, on the side of the Isthmus that faces Athens, he puts a fish perhaps fifteen feet long with the head and mouth of a bird. Its scales, he says, you would take for the feathers of a crane. The Isthmus is a morning's walk from cities full of fishermen, and the sea-crane of Corinth appears in no other ancient author who has come down to us. It is an exceedingly powerful jumper, and when it goes it springs forward like an arrow shot from a bowstring.
suggested_refs: Isthmia and the Corinthian gulf waters of On Animals 15.9
sources: Aelian, On the Characteristics of Animals 15.9, https://www.attalus.org/translate/animals15.html
Wikipedia, 'Isthmia (ancient city)', for the coordinate

stops.name: Delphi, the deer with four horns
stops.date_confidence: Text attested at On Animals 11.40; the dedication it reports belongs to Nicocreon of Cyprus in the fourth century BC. Date is the composition window.
stops.campa: Nicocreon of Cyprus takes a deer with four horns and sends it to Delphi as an offering, with a verse cut for it crediting Apollo with the capture. The god who governs prophecy receives an animal whose body is itself outside the ordinary count. Aelian collects the dedication in the same chapter as the Alexandrian ox and the Paphlagonian partridges, one item in a catalogue of bodies that came out with too many parts. What he records is the number of horns and the name of the man who sent them.
suggested_refs: Nicocreon of Cyprus and the Delphic dedications of the fourth century BC
sources: Aelian, On the Characteristics of Animals 11.40, https://www.attalus.org/translate/animals11.html

stops.name: The Acropolis, sheep in the temple of Zeus Polieus
stops.date_confidence: Text attested at On Animals 11.40, but the city is not. Many Greek cities kept a cult of Zeus Polieus; the Athenian altar on the Acropolis, site of the Bouphonia, is the best-attested and is used here as an illustrative pin. Aelian never went to Athens.
stops.campa: In the temple of Zeus Polieus, Guardian of the City, there were sheep with four horns, and sheep with three. He gives it in a single clause and moves straight on. The temple is not assigned to a city, because the cult stands in many cities and the reader is expected to supply the nearest one. What matters to the chapter is that the surplus horn turns up in a sanctuary, on an animal kept for sacrifice, where priests would have counted it. Nothing is said about what the count was taken to mean.
suggested_refs: The altar of Zeus Polieus on the Athenian Acropolis and the rite of the Bouphonia
sources: Aelian, On the Characteristics of Animals 11.40, https://www.attalus.org/translate/animals11.html

stops.name: Sinope, the partridges with two hearts
stops.date_confidence: Text attested at On Animals 11.40, attributed there to Theophrastus. The pin is editorial: Aelian names Paphlagonia and no town, and Sinope is its chief port.
stops.campa: Theophrastus, who took over Aristotle's school at Athens, wrote that the partridges of Paphlagonia are born with two hearts. Aelian copies the report five centuries later with the name of the man who made it still attached. This is the whole of his procedure: the marvel and the authority for it set side by side, so that a reader who will not believe the one knows exactly whom to disbelieve. Neither man is recorded as having gone to Paphlagonia to open a partridge.
suggested_refs: Theophrastus, the lost zoological works quarried by later compilers
sources: Aelian, On the Characteristics of Animals 11.40, https://www.attalus.org/translate/animals11.html

stops.name: Bisaltia, the hares with a double liver
stops.date_confidence: Text attested at On Animals 11.40, attributed there to Theopompus. The pin is Amphipolis, standing for the Macedonian and Thracian region of Bisaltia; no town is named in the text.
stops.campa: Theopompus of Chios reported that the hares in Bisaltia have each of them a double liver. The country lies in Macedonian Thrace north of the Strymon, and the claim is the kind a hunter could settle in an afternoon. It stands in the chapter beside the two-hearted partridges and the sheep with the extra horns, in a run of notices that keeps finding the body with one part too many, region after region, across five hundred years of Greek writing. He names Theopompus for it and copies the claim across.
suggested_refs: Theopompus of Chios, the fourth-century historian whose marvels reached the imperial compilers
sources: Aelian, On the Characteristics of Animals 11.40, https://www.attalus.org/translate/animals11.html

segments.name: Severan Rome and the Indictment of Gynnis

stops.name: Castra Praetoria, the emperor killed in the camp
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day by the standard Roman chronology and used by Philostratus's translator to date the following episode. Aelian is not placed at the camp; this stop marks the external event that anchors the only dated point in his life.
stops.campa: The Praetorians kill the emperor inside their own camp on the northeast edge of the city, and his mother with him. Elagabalus is eighteen. The bodies are dragged through the streets and put into the Tiber, the name is struck from the records, and Rome is invited to agree that the four years just past were an aberration rather than a reign. Aelian is somewhere in the city, past fifty, with a manuscript. Nothing places him at the camp or anywhere else that day. The date is the thirteenth of March, 222, and it is the only fixed point in his biography.
suggested_refs: The Castra Praetoria, Rome, and the damnatio memoriae of Elagabalus
sources: Wilmer Cave Wright, translator's note to Philostratus, Lives of the Sophists 2.31, Loeb 134 (1922), identifying Gynnis as Heliogabalus, 'who was put to death in 222'
Wikipedia, 'Castra Praetoria', for the coordinate

stops.name: Rome, the Indictment read aloud
stops.date_confidence: The scene is attested at Philostratus, VS 2.31; the month is not. Philostratus places it after the tyrant's death, which Wright's note fixes to 13 March 222, so April is an ordering choice inside the weeks that follow. The venue is unspecified in the source; the Athenaeum of Hadrian is a modern guess and is not used as the pin.
stops.campa: Philostratus of Lemnos finds him holding a book and reading it out in an indignant and emphatic voice. Asked what has him so worked up, Aelian says he has composed an Indictment of Gynnis: the Womanish One, his name for the tyrant just put to death, whose wanton wickedness had disgraced the empire. It is the only thing anyone records him doing in public across fifty years of a public profession. The text is lost entire. He is still holding the book, still reading out of it, when the other man answers him.
stops.quote: I have composed an indictment of Gynnis
stops.quote_source: Aelian, quoted at Philostratus, Lives of the Sophists 2.31, trans. Wilmer Cave Wright, Loeb 134 (1922), p. 305
suggested_refs: The lost Indictment of Gynnis, known only from this anecdote
Steven D. Smith, Man and Animal in Severan Rome (Cambridge, 2014), proposing a link between the lost On the Syrian Mime and the Gynnis indictment
sources: Philostratus, Lives of the Sophists 2.31 (Wright, Loeb 134, 1922), p. 305, archive.org identifier philostratuseuna00phil

stops.name: Rome, the answer of Philostratus of Lemnos
stops.date_confidence: Same scene, same source, immediately following. The day is an ordering device only. In Wright's text only the first clause of the retort is direct speech; the rest is reported indirectly and is paraphrased here rather than quoted.
stops.campa: The answer comes back at once, and Philostratus preserves it as the pivot of the whole notice. Admiration would have been owed for an indictment written while the man was alive; it takes something to curb a living tyrant, and anyone at all can trample one already down. Aelian, who has spent a working life declining to perform, is caught performing courage at the safest possible moment. He is not recorded as answering. No other ancient writer mentions the Indictment, and no line of it survives.
stops.quote: I should admire you for it, if you had indicted him while he was alive.
stops.quote_source: Philostratus of Lemnos to Aelian, at Philostratus, Lives of the Sophists 2.31, trans. Wilmer Cave Wright, Loeb 134 (1922)
suggested_refs: Philostratus of Lemnos, the sophist who reports the exchange to his kinsman the biographer
sources: Philostratus, Lives of the Sophists 2.31 (Wright, Loeb 134, 1922), p. 305

segments.name: The Epilogue and the Silence After It

stops.name: Rome, the meadow rather than the catalogue
stops.date_confidence: The prologue and epilogue are attested as parts of the finished seventeen books; no year of completion is recorded anywhere. The date orders the segment. The Loeb introduction reports a tradition that the Varia Historia, the other surviving work, still needed revision at his death and was released by his executors; that tradition is not independently verified here.
stops.campa: Seventeen books are finished, with a prologue at the front and an epilogue at the back defending the way they are arranged, which is to say not arranged at all. He puts the elephant beside the sea-urchin and India beside Boeotia, and calls the principle poikilia, variegation, the quality of a meadow rather than of a catalogue. The order is deliberate and he says so twice, once at each end, because he expects to be accused of having none. He has collected what he could, he says, and clothed it in untechnical language.
stops.quote: I have collected all the materials that I could; I have clothed them in untechnical language, and am persuaded that my achievement is a treasure far from negligible.
stops.quote_source: Aelian, On the Characteristics of Animals, prologue to Book 1, trans. A. F. Scholfield, via Attalus.org
suggested_refs: Aelian, On Animals, prologue and epilogue, the defence of the non-sequential arrangement
Alexandra Trachsel and Hendrik Muller, eds., Claudius Aelianus: Quotation Practices and Literary Skills of an Imperial Collector of Knowledge (Franz Steiner, 2025)
sources: Aelian, On the Characteristics of Animals, prologue, https://www.attalus.org/translate/animals1.html
N. G. Wilson, introduction to Aelian, Historical Miscellany, Loeb 486 (1997)

stops.name: Rome, foxes and lizards instead of palaces
stops.date_confidence: Text attested in the epilogue to Book 17; undated. The date orders the segment inside the composition window.
stops.campa: At the close of the seventeenth book he sets out what he did not do with his life. He might have given himself airs, appeared in palaces, come into considerable wealth, and the road was open: the men who took it are all around him in Severan Rome. He occupied himself instead with foxes and lizards and beetles and snakes and lions. He would rather have expert knowledge of one branch of anything than the splendid riches of the wealthiest men in the city. That is where the seventeenth book ends.
stops.quote: I however occupy myself with foxes and lizards and beetles and snakes and lions... I would rather attain to expert knowledge in at least one branch than to the splendid riches and possessions of your wealthiest men.
stops.quote_source: Aelian, On the Characteristics of Animals, epilogue to Book 17, trans. A. F. Scholfield, via Attalus.org
suggested_refs: Steven D. Smith, Man and Animal in Severan Rome (Cambridge, 2014), reading the epilogue as disavowal rather than modesty
sources: Aelian, On the Characteristics of Animals, book 17 epilogue, https://www.attalus.org/translate/animals17.html
Bryn Mawr Classical Review 2015.09.15 (C. W. Marshall) on Smith's reading

stops.name: Rome, over sixty, and no children
stops.date_confidence: Death year unknown. Philostratus attests only that he lived past sixty and died childless, having never married. Modern handbooks give c. 230-235 with an outer range to c. 238; Wikipedia gives c. 235. The place is a modern inference: no ancient source says where he died, and Rome is used here as the default. Month and day defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: He lives past sixty and dies leaving no children, having never married; Philostratus puts it as an evasion, that by never marrying he got out of begetting. No year is recorded, no illness, no last words, no city. The handbooks settle on the middle of the 230s because the Indictment fixes him alive in the spring of 222 and the sixty-odd years have to fit somewhere behind that. His own books say nothing about any of it, and the Suda knows his nickname and not his death. Where he was when he died, and of what, nobody has ever established.
stops.quote: He lived to be over sixty years of age and died leaving no children; for by never marrying he evaded begetting children.
stops.quote_source: Philostratus, Lives of the Sophists 2.31, trans. Wilmer Cave Wright, Loeb 134 (1922), p. 307
suggested_refs: Philostratus, Lives of the Sophists 2.31, the only near-contemporary notice of his death
sources: Philostratus, Lives of the Sophists 2.31 (Wright, Loeb 134, 1922), p. 307
Wikipedia, 'Aelian (writer)', giving c. 175 - c. 235

stops.name: Rome, no tomb and no face
stops.date_confidence: This stop records an absence rather than an event, and the date is an ordering device. Confirmed by exhaustion of the two surviving testimonia rather than by any positive source: neither Philostratus nor the Suda mentions a tomb, a monument, a funeral or an image, and no inscription, portrait or document naming him has been located.
stops.campa: There is no tomb. No grave marker, no epitaph, no inscription anywhere naming Claudius Aelianus, no property record, no letter, no bust that can be shown to be him. His entire biography comes out of two texts: four sentences in a Byzantine encyclopedia and two pages in Philostratus. Everything else is inference from twenty-three books about animals and about other people's sayings. Twenty-three books survive, and one Byzantine encyclopedia entry, and two pages of a biographer. Nothing else has been found.
suggested_refs: The absence of any epigraphic or iconographic record for Aelian, a gap noted rather than filled
sources: Suda On Line, entry alpha-iota 178
Philostratus, Lives of the Sophists 2.31 (Wright, Loeb 134, 1922)

stops.name: Constantinople, the encyclopedia that keeps the fragments
stops.date_confidence: This stop marks where his text survives, not a place he went: Aelian is seven centuries dead by the Suda's compilation, conventionally placed in the late tenth century. The Suda's own entry on him is four sentences and names no works; the titles On Providence and On Divine Manifestations come from the Suda On Line editorial notes and standard reference literature, not from the entry itself. The Manuel Philes connection rests on Kindstrand's 1986 article, which was not independently consulted.
stops.campa: The Suda, compiled by people who could still read him whole, quotes him so heavily that the two lost works, On Providence and On Divine Manifestations, survive only in the pieces its compilers cut out. Its own entry on him runs to four sentences. Manuel Philes, writing verse in the same city three centuries later, takes the animal material and works it into a poem of his own. What reaches the modern world reaches it through this city, in pieces, quoted by people who were making something else.
suggested_refs: J. F. Kindstrand, 'Manuel Philes' Use of Aelian's De natura animalium in his De animalium proprietate', Studi italiani di filologia classica 4 (1986): 119-139
Manuel Philes, De animalium proprietate
sources: Suda On Line, entry alpha-iota 178 and its editorial notes
Kindstrand 1986, cited at second hand; the article is not open access and was not read

stops.name: Rome, the first printing
stops.date_confidence: Year attested; month and day not recorded and defaulted to 01-01. This stop marks an event in the life of the text, not of the man, who is some thirteen centuries dead.
stops.campa: Thirteen centuries after he wrote it, the Varia Historia is set in type for the first time, at Rome, by the printer Antonio Blado, from manuscripts including a codex in the Vatican library. Camillo Peruschi, bishop of Alatri, prepares the copy. The city where he taught rhetoric and read his indictment aloud is the city that prints him first, and the fourteen books of anecdotes go out into a Europe that begins quarrying them for material. The year is 1545.
suggested_refs: Codex Vaticanus graecus 1375, among the manuscript sources of the 1545 edition
A surviving 1545 Blado copy bound for Colonel Thomas Wildman of Newstead Abbey (53.0783, -1.1925) and later acquired by the University of Rochester through the bibliographer Robert F. Metzdorf
Thomas Stanley, Claudius Aelianus His Various History (London, 1665), the first English translation
